edges.description: Loss of asparagine synthetase activity impairs de novo asparagine synthesis, which is critical in the brain.
Cerebral asparagine deficiency impairs neural progenitor function and cortical growth.
intermediate_mechanisms: High ASNS expression in cortical plate neurons and ventricular/subventricular-zone neural progenitors.
Dependence of cortical neurogenesis and brain growth on endogenous asparagine synthesis.

intermediate_mechanisms: Diffuse neuronal loss and astrocytic gliosis.

evidence.snippet: ASNS encodes the glutamine-dependent asparagine synthetase enzyme (EC 6.3.5.4), which catalyzes ammonia transfer from glutamine to aspartic acid via a β-aspartyl-AMP intermediate.

nodes.description: Biallelic ASNS pathogenic variants (missense changes that reduce protein abundance or catalytic performance) abolish or diminish asparagine synthetase activity. ASNS is the glutamine-dependent enzyme (EC 6.3.5.4) that transfers ammonia from glutamine to aspartate to synthesize asparagine; loss of this activity is the initiating molecular lesion in ASNSD.

nodes.description: An alternative, non-exclusive mechanistic hypothesis: with asparagine synthesis blocked, the substrates aspartate and glutamate accumulate, and the resulting excitatory-amino-acid excess is proposed to cause enhanced neuronal excitability and excitotoxic damage. This overlaps mechanistically with pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy, where cytotoxic glutamate accumulation is implicated, and helps explain the severe epileptic encephalopathy.

nodes.description: Because asparagine crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and ASNS is highly expressed in the brain, loss of enzyme activity produces a functional cerebral asparagine deficiency with a concomitant rise in the unused substrates glutamine and aspartate. Although asparagine is a non-essential amino acid systemically, its endogenous synthesis is required for normal brain development and function.

nodes.description: ASNS is enriched in cortical-plate neurons and in the ventricular and subventricular-zone neural progenitors of the developing cerebral cortex. Deficient asparagine synthesis in these cells impairs cortical neurogenesis and brain growth, in a pattern resembling other microcephaly genes, producing congenital and progressive microcephaly. A hypomorphic Asns mouse model shows reduced cortical thickness and enlarged ventricles.
